newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's new economic pact wins mixed reviews.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's new economic pact wins mixed reviews.

text.p: Mexico's 1997 economic program has won high marks from economists who view it as an orthodox recipe for recovery, but it was given a more muted reception on Monday from ordinary Mexicans battered by two years of crisis.

Officially dubbed the Alliance for Economic Growth (ACE), the plan unveiled Saturday was seen as more of the same from Yale-educated President Ernesto Zedillo -- a by-the-books free-market policy that tries to nudge a sluggish economy forward without risking higher inflation or the wrath of financial markets.

The plan, agreed in advance with business and labor, calls for economic growth next year of four percent and inflation of 15 percent, compared to growth of about 3.5 percent this year and inflation of some 26 percent.

Eager to spur growth outside the booming export sector and anxious to quell new guerrilla movements, Mexican officials trumpeted the plan as the best for workers since the 1994 peso crash caused the worst recession in decades.
The plan gives tax breaks for business, calls for a small real increase in the minimum wage and plans a budget deficit for the first time in years at some 0.5 percent of gross domestic product.
Even the plan's new name -- replacing last year's Alliance for Economic Recovery -- shows the government wants to emphasize a more pro-growth strategy, economists said.

Although they praised the overall plan, many economists doubted the government could deliver on a promised increase in real wages. The plan raises the minimum wage by 17 percent, but economists think inflation will climb higher than the 15 percent target.
"We are expecting about 18 percent inflation next year," said Javier Maldonado, an economist at Bancomer, one of Mexico's largest banks.
Mexico's financial markets gave the plan only two cheers, despite expectations the markets would rally after it cleared up uncertainty about future economic policy.
The benchmark 48-hour peso was up 1.75 centavos at 7.905/7.915 per dollar, still near its 11-month lows reached on Friday. The stock market's leading IPC index was off some 14 points to 3,218.
Dealers said investors may be reluctant to invest in Mexico because of lingering concern that the average consumer will be unable to fuel an economic recovery.
Ordinary Mexicans also greeted the plan with a healthy dose of skepticism.
"It has a new name ... but it's the same old thing, a recipe where workers' salaries have been the big loser," wrote business columnist Alberto Aguilar in Mexico City's Reforma newspaper.
Reforma said that in the nine years since the pact was introduced by then-President Miguel de la Madrid, the minimum wage has grown 404.4 percent while inflation has been 761.7 percent.
Politically, the plan is viewed as a victory for Zedillo, who managed to avoid the bitter wrangling that preceded the government's first attempt at an economic agreement after the devaluation.

"The fact that they can wheel out labor and business sectors for this shows there is still a degree of consensus in Mexico regarding economic policy," said Damian Fraser, director of Caspian Research brokerage firm in Mexico City.
